t: #4028 Minimum Operations to Make a Rotated Palindrome II — Evaluate Every Rotation
o: A left rotation by r turns s into t; making t a palindrome costs, for each mirrored pair, the minimum number of cyclic letter increments to equalize the two letters (we may push either one). The answer is the cheapest rotation. Example 1: rotating "abc" gives "bca", whose outer pair (b,a) needs 1 increment → 2 total. Example 2: "yb" needs 3 increments on the first character. With n up to 5·10⁴ there are n rotations, each costing O(n) to score — the crux is scoring each rotation as cheaply as possible and pruning hopeless ones early.
k: Rotation r pairs positions (r+i) and (r+n−1−i); the cost of a pair is the cyclic alphabet distance min(d, 26−d).
Precomputing a 26×26 distance table (or just taking min(|a−b|, 26−|a−b|)) makes each pair O(1).
Early termination once the partial cost reaches the best-so-far prunes most rotations in practice.

a.i: For each rotation r, walk the ⌊n/2⌋ mirrored pairs of the rotated string, add cyclic distances, and keep the minimum. Doubling the array removes modulo operations in the inner loop.
s: Map letters to 0..25 and build b = a + a (doubled).
For each rotation r, sum min(|b[r+i] − b[r+n−1−i]|, 26 − that) over i < n/2.
Return the minimum total over all r.
a.t: O(n²) — n rotations, each scored over n/2 pairs with O(1) work per pair.

a.i: Same iteration order, but abandon a rotation as soon as its accumulated cost reaches the current best — its final cost cannot improve the answer. Random-ish inputs prune aggressively; adversarial inputs (e.g., all 'a') degrade gracefully to the full scan, which is then trivially cheap per pair.
s: Build the doubled array as before and initialize best = infinity.
For each rotation, accumulate pair costs but break out immediately once cost ≥ best.
Only record best when a rotation finishes under the old bound; return best.
a.t: O(n²) worst case, typically far less — pruning aborts rotations once they exceed the incumbent best.

w: Start from the direct scorer, then add pruning — interviewers like seeing the bound-based cutoff. Pitfalls: forgetting the wrap-around 'z'→'a' (handled by min(d, 26−d)), double-counting the middle character of odd-length strings (loop only to n/2), and integer overflow (costs fit easily in int here, but verify: ≤ 13n/2). Follow-ups: allow decrements too (same cost model), or ask which rotation achieves the optimum.
